newsitem.title: INDIA: India closes border with Nepal for state poll.
newsitem.headline: India closes border with Nepal for state poll.

text.p: Indian security forces sealed off the land border between the state of Uttar Pradesh and Nepal on Monday as the third phase of crucial assembly polls got underway.
"The Nepal border is often used by anti-social elements," a state government official told Reuters. "We have taken this temporary step to enable peaceful polling in the border areas."

State officials said tens of thousands of paramilitary forces were deployed to monitor 124 contests in India's most populous state in what was due to be the last phase of polling for the state assembly's 425 seats.
Voting in five constituencies was put back to October 9. The delay in at least three cases was due to violence, including Hindu-Moslem clashes in the state capital Lucknow.
With 140 million people, sprawling Uttar Pradesh is larger than France and more populous than Japan or Pakistan.
The state shares a porous 700-km (420-mile) border with land-locked Nepal. Indian officials say the border with the Himalayan Kingdom is also used by smugglers and fugitives.
Uttar Pradesh has a smaller border with Tibet which was opened recently for modest cross-border trade with China.
Security officials said another border between Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, India's second most populous state, could be a source of trouble.
Both Bihar and Uttar Pradesh have a history of violent elections.
At least 16 people were killed in poll-related violence in the month-long campaign for the Uttar Pradesh assembly involving 90 million registered voters.

Politicians said the election tests Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's ability to ride out a challenge by the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), India's main opposition group. The BJP is pushing for mid-term parliamentary polls.

The assembly polls have seen Deve Gowda's fractious United Front alliance take on the Congress party, which supports his minority government in Delhi, and the BJP, in a triangular fight for the state Vidhan Sabha, or lower house.
Uttar Pradesh sends 85 deputies to the 545-member federal parliament, where the BJP is the single biggest party.

The BJP enjoys wide support in Uttar Pradesh. The party's campaign to build a Hindu temple on the site of a 16th century mosque catapulted it to power in several north Indian states and made it the main opposition party in parliament in 1991.

Militant supporters of the BJP demolished the Babri mosque in Ayodhya, 200 km (120 miles) east of Lucknow, in December 1992. Their action triggered nationwide Hindu-Moslem riots in which more than 3,000 people died.
Hindu militants claim two more mosques, in the western Uttar Pradesh city of Mathura and in Varanasi on the state's eastern flank, saying they stand on sites of ancient Hindu temples.

While the BJP played down the issue in its campaign, the government, taking no chances, staggered the polls over three days to ensure voting near each of the three disputed sites was conducted on different days.

Analysts say the state, once a bastion of the Congress party which ruled India for all but four years since independence in 1947, could follow a recent trend of coalition politics that helped Deve Gowda form a minority government in June.
